abstract.p: A combination of Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor ibrutinib and rituximab has shown promising efficacy in mantle cell lymphoma (MCL). This phase II trial evaluated the second-generation BTK inhibitor zanubrutinib plus rituximab as induction, followed by shortened chemoimmunotherapy as frontline treatment for MCL (NCT04624958). Eligible patients had histologically confirmed stage II–IV disease requiring immediate therapy and no prior MCL-related systemic treatment. Patients received zanubrutinib-rituximab for up to 12 cycles (part A); those achieving a complete response (CR) or experiencing disease progression proceeded to four cycles of R-DHAOx (rituximab, dexamethasone, cytarabine, and oxaliplatin) (part B). Patients with CR after part B received zanubrutinib maintenance for one year. The primary endpoint was the CR rate at part A completion. Forty-two patients were enrolled. The CR rate at part A completion was 88% (95% confidence interval [CI], 74-96), and 86% (95% CI, 72-95) at part B completion. Hematologic toxicities predominated: the most common grade 3-4 adverse events were neutropenia (7%) in part A, and thrombocytopenia (77%) and neutropenia (49%) in part B. In conclusion, zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by shortened R-DHAOx is efficacious with manageable safety as frontline therapy for MCL. This strategy allows for a reduction in chemotherapy cycles and warrants validation in randomized controlled trials.

Zanubrutinib is a second-generation BTK inhibitor, reported to have fewer off-target toxicities while maintaining comparable efficacy to previous BTK inhibitors. Here, the authors report the phase II CHESS trial evaluating frontline Zanubrutinib (second-generation BTK inhibitor) plus rituximab (anti-CD20) induction, followed by chemoimmunotherapy in patients with mantle cell lymphoma.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), a subtype of mature B-cell lymphoma, is characterized by translocation of t(11;14)(q13;q32) and cyclin D1 overexpression1. The standard of care aggressive therapy for MCL is cytarabine-based chemoimmunotherapy regimens, such as the LyMa regimen (rituximab, dexamethasone, cytarabine, and platinum [R-DHAP] × 4 cycles followed by rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, and prednisone [R-CHOP] × 4 cycles in non-complete response [CR] patients)2, the NORDIC regimen (dose-intensified R-CHOP alternating with rituximab and high-dose cytarabine × 6 cycles)3, R-CHOP + ibrutinib alternating with R-DHAP × 6 cycles4, rituximab and bendamustine (BR) × 3 cycles followed by rituximab and high-dose cytarabine × 3 cycles5, with optional autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) and maintenance therapy. For patients not suitable for aggressive induction therapies and ASCT, several less aggressive regimens without high-dose cytarabine, such as bortezomib, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisone (VR-CAP) regimen6, BR regimen7, BR + acalabrutinib regimen8, are recommended. Although cytarabine plays a significant role in the frontline treatment of MCL, the aforementioned cytarabine-based regimens are associated with significant myelosuppression and an increased risk of secondary malignancies4,5,9,10.

Treatment of MCL has been revolutionized by Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors during the past decade11–15. Several trials have shown the promising efficacy of combining BTK inhibitors and rituximab as frontline treatment in MCL patients with older age or indolent disease16–20. In the WINDOW-1 trial, the BTK inhibitor ibrutinib and rituximab as induction therapy followed by shortened R-HCVAD (rituximab, hyper-fractionated cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, and dexamethasone) alternating with R-methotrexate-cytarabine regimen in previously untreated MCL patients resulted in 87% complete response (CR) rate after induction and 89% CR rate after R-HCVAD regimen21.

Compared with ibrutinib, the second-generation BTK inhibitor zanubrutinib has higher selectivity for BTK and thus fewer off-target toxicities22–24. In comparison to ibrutinib, zanubrutinib demonstrated less cardiovascular toxicity and a lower rate of treatment discontinuation with comparable efficacy in phase 3 trials25,26. In a phase 2 trial for relapsed or refractory MCL, zanubrutinib achieved 78% CR rate and a 33-month median progression-free survival (PFS)13. Considering the favorable efficacy and safety profile, using zanubrutinib as a frontline treatment may represent a promising approach.

We conducted this phase II trial (CHESS) to evaluate the safety and efficacy of zanubrutinib plus rituximab as induction therapy, followed by a shortened course of chemoimmunotherapy in previously untreated MCL patients. R-DHAOx regimen (rituximab, dexamethasone, cytarabine, and oxaliplatin) was selected based on its proven efficacy in clinical practice and several key factors: (1) improved outcomes of adding high-dose cytarabine to chemoimmunotherapy27; (2) a high CR rate (77%) in the LyMa trial with the R-DHA-platinum regimen2, which is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guideline; (3) a tendency for longer disease control duration observed with oxaliplatin in subgroup analyses of the LyMa trial compared to cisplatin and carboplatin28; and (4) Given that the potential overlapping toxicity of thrombocytopenia in high-dose cytarabine and carboplatin, as well as lower nephrotoxicity and ease of administration with oxaliplatin than cisplatin29,30, we chose oxaliplatin as the platinum used in our regimen. In this work, we show that zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by shortened chemoimmunotherapy yields promising efficacy and an acceptable safety profile as frontline treatment for MCL. Based on transcriptome features, we identified three molecular subtypes that correlate with treatment response and survival outcomes.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p:
Between December 1, 2020, and December 13, 2023, 42 patients were enrolled. Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The median age was 57 years (interquartile range [IQR], 51–64), and 35 patients (83%) were male. Based on tumor tissue samples, Ki-67 was ≥ 30% in 29 (69%) patients; histological subtype was blastoid/pleomorphic in 5 (12%) patients. The risk based on the simplified Mantle Cell Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (sMIPI) was low, intermediate, and high in 24 (57%), 15 (36%), and 3 (7%) patients, respectively. Minimal residual disease (MRD) in bone marrow was detected in 36 (86%) patients. In the 35 patients with known MRD status in peripheral blood, the bone marrow and peripheral blood results were concordant except in one patient (positive in bone marrow but negative in peripheral blood) (Supplementary Table 1). In the six patients without bone marrow involvement at baseline, none had detectable MRD in peripheral blood, and they underwent MRD detection only in peripheral blood in subsequent time points.Table 1

sec.title: Response
sec.p:
The median treatment cycle in part A was 4 (IQR, 4–4), and all 42 patients were evaluable for response. For the evaluation of the primary endpoint, 37 (88%; 95% CI, 74–96) patients achieved CR at part A completion. The remaining five patients (12% [95% CI, 4–26]) experienced disease progression (Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1). CR was confirmed by 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography (PET) in all patients, plus bone marrow biopsy in patients with bone marrow involvement at baseline. Detailed information on the patients with progressive disease (PD) is provided in Supplementary Table 2. The best overall response rate (ORR) and CR rate was 98% (95% CI, 87–100) and 88% (95% CI, 74–96), respectively. The median time to CR was four months (IQR, 4–4). MRD was negative at part A completion in 33 patients (Supplementary Table 1), and the MRD-negative CR rate was 74% (31/42; 95% CI, 58–86). The dynamic change of MRD and its relationship with treatment response are presented in Supplementary Fig. 2. In post-hoc subgroup analyses, the CR rate at part A completion was 40% (2/5) in patients with blastoid/pleomorphic disease and 95% (35/37) in those with classic/small cell disease; 33% (1/3) in patients with TP53 mutation and 94% (32/34) in those with wild type TP53. There were no obvious differences in other subgroups, including age, sex, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, stage, bone marrow involvement, lactate dehydrogenase, Ki-67 and sMIPI risk (Supplementary Table 2).Table 2

Thirty-nine patients proceeded to part B treatment with R-DHAOx regimen. At part B completion, among the 39 patients, the CR rate was 92% (36/39; 95% CI, 79–98), and disease progressed in the remaining three patients (8%; 3/39; 95% CI, 2–21; all had PD in part A) (Table 2). Thirty-six of the 37 patients with CR at part A completion remained in CR and had undetectable MRD at part B completion (Fig. S2 and Table S1); one patient was lost to follow-up after part A.

For the overall response following part B completion, 36 patients achieved CR (86% [95% CI, 72–95]), three patients had PD (7% [95% CI, 2–20], and three patients were not evaluable due to not receiving part B treatment. In post-hoc subgroup analyses, the CR rate at part B completion was 40% (2/5) in patients with blastoid/pleomorphic disease and 92% (34/37) in those with classic/small cell disease; 33% (1/3) in patients with TP53 mutation and 91% (31/34) in those with wild-type TP53 (Table S2). There were no significant differences in other subgroups.

sec.title: Survival outcomes
sec.p:
With a median follow-up of 23 months (IQR, 14-29), the median PFS and overall survival (OS) were not reached. The analysis of the median PFS and OS was planned, but the data were immature. The 2-year PFS and OS rate was 85% (95% CI, 75–97) and 90% (95% CI, 75–100), respectively (Fig. 2A, B). The median duration of response (DoR) was 17 months (IQR, 8-23). Five patients experienced disease progression, and three patients died due to lymphoma progression; all were non-CR patients in part A. Detailed clinical information and salvage therapies of the five PD patients in the current trial are summarized in Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary Table 4. None of the 37 patients with CR at the completion of part A had disease progression; one died of COVID-19 pneumonia. Patients with blastoid/pleomorphic disease had inferior survival outcomes than those with classic/small cell disease (Supplementary Figs. 3A and 4A). Patients with TP53 mutations had inferior PFS, but no OS difference was observed. Neither PFS nor OS differed between the patients with different age (<60 vs ≥ 60 years), stage (II vs III-IV), Ki-67 (<30% vs ≥ 30%), or sMIPI risk (low vs intermediate vs high risk) (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4).Fig. 2Survival outcomes.
A Median PFS was not reached; the 2-year PFS was 85% (95% CI, 75–97). B Median OS was not reached; the 2-year OS was 90% (95% CI, 75–100). CI confidence interval, PFS progression-free survival, OS overall survival.

sec.title: Adverse events
sec.p:
In part A, the most common treatment-related AEs (TRAEs) were neutropenia (11 [26%] of 42 patients), fatigue (11 [26%]), lymphocytopenia (11 [26%]), and rash (9 [21%]) (Table 3). Hemorrhage (all grade 1 or 2) occurred in four (10%) patients. The most common grade 3-4 TRAEs were neutropenia (3 [7%]) and lymphocytopenia (3 [7%]). No patient needed zanubrutinib dose reduction in part A. Zanubrutinib dose suspension was required in five (12%) of 42 patients (three patients for neutropenia, one for infection, and one for elevated liver enzymes). None of the patients needed recombinant human granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (rhG-CSF) supportive treatment during part A. There were no treatment-related deaths.Table 3

In part B, grade 3-4 events were predominantly hematological. The most common grade 3-4 TRAE was thrombocytopenia (30 [77%] in 39 patients), followed by leukocytopenia (23 [59%]), and neutropenia (19 [49%]) (Table 3). The most common non-hematological TRAEs were elevated liver enzymes (20 [51%]) and fatigue (20 [51%]), but most were grade 1-2. Dose reduction of chemotherapeutic agents was required in 32 (82%) of 39 patients due to toxicities (27 patients for thrombocytopenia, four for neutropenia, and one for elevated liver enzymes). Of these, 25 patients had their dose of cytarabine reduced by one dose level to 75% of the original dose, and seven patients required a reduction of two dose levels to 50%.

Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (TPO-RAs) or recombinant human thrombopoietin (rhTPO) were given in 9 patients as primary prevention for thrombocytopenia, and in 13 patients as secondary prevention. Five patients still experienced severe thrombocytopenia despite supportive care with TPO-RAs or rhTPO and dose reduction, and therefore discontinued treatment. rhG-CSF was given in 26 patients as primary prevention for neutropenia, and in all 19 patients who had experienced grade 3-4 neutropenia as secondary prevention. None of the patients experienced further occurrence of severe neutropenia after receiving rhG-CSF supportive therapy and dose reduction. Chemotherapy dose suspension was required in 20 (51%) of 39 patients due to toxicities (18 patients for thrombocytopenia, one for neutropenia, and one for elevated liver enzymes). Five patients discontinued chemotherapy permanently due to toxicities (all due to grade 4 thrombocytopenia). There were no treatment-related deaths.

TRAEs in the zanubrutinib maintenance phase are summarized in Table 3. One patient experienced grade 3 neutropenia and recovered after supportive treatment with rhG-CSF, after which the zanubrutinib dose was reduced to 80 mg twice daily. No other dose reductions were required during the maintenance phase. Zanubrutinib dose suspension was required in six (18%) of 34 patients (two patients for neutropenia, two patients for fatigue, and one patient each for thrombocytopenia and infections). No patient required treatment discontinuation.

This trial was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic. One patient died from COVID-19 pneumonia and respiratory failure during part B. A total of 30 patients tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 at least once, and 17 patients required treatment suspension due to SARS-CoV-2 infection.

sec.title: Transcriptional and genomic analyses
sec.p:
Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) based on bulk RNA sequencing in 37 available tumor tissue samples at baseline revealed three MCL molecular subtypes (M1-M3) (Fig. 3A). M1 (n = 4) was characterized by activation of cell-cycle pathways, including G2M pathways, E2F targets, MYC targets and DNA replication (Figs. 3B and S5A). M2 (n = 26) was characterized by activation and regulation of T cells (T cell activation, T cell antigen processing and presentation, and T cell co-stimulation) and DNA repair (Fig. 3B). M3 (n = 7) was characterized by upregulation of inflammatory pathways (e.g., JAK-STAT3 signaling and TNF-α signaling) (Fig. 3B and Supplementary Fig. 5A). Activation of specific pathways (e.g., hypoxia, angiogenesis, extracellular matrix organization, and cell matrix adhesion) and the increased infiltration of stromal cells and immunosuppressive cells (cancer-associated fibroblasts and myeloid-derived suppressor cells) (Supplementary Fig. 5B) indicated a more complex tumor microenvironment in M3. The genomic profiles, including mutated genes and tumor mutation burden in each molecular subtype, are presented in Supplementary Fig. 6.Fig. 3Molecular subtypes of MCL.

None of the four patients of the M1 subtype achieved CR in part A; all four patients experienced PD within 9 months and died within 24 months (Fig. 3C, D). In contrast, all patients of the M2 subtype obtained early-CR. In the seven patients of the M3 subtype, two achieved early-CR and the remaining five achieved late-CR (Fig. 3C). The distribution of histological subtypes, sMIPI risk, and Ki-67 in different molecular subtypes are presented in Supplementary Fig. 5C. In the 24 patients of the M2 subtype with positive MRD at baseline, MRD became undetectable in all 24 patients at the completion of part A. In contrast, the MRD status remained unchanged from baseline to part A completion in all patients of the M1 and M3 subtypes (Fig. 3E).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This trial demonstrated a high CR rate with manageable toxicity using zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by shortened chemoimmunotherapy in previously untreated MCL patients. Three molecular subtypes based on transcriptome features were identified and correlated with treatment response and survival outcomes.

Currently, most of the cytarabine-based chemotherapy regimens, such as the NORDIC regimen10, alternating R-CHOP/R-DHAP regimen4,27, and R-hyper-CVAD/R-high dose methotrexate and cytarabine regimen31, contain six to eight cycles of treatment. The current trial used a shortened four cycles of R-DHAOx regimen. Notably, the LyMa trial2 also used four cycles of R-DHAP, but the intensity of the overall treatment was ensured by routine consolidation therapy with HDT/ASCT, additional four cycles of R-CHOP for PR patients, and one cycle of the CVP regimen was allowed before study treatment. In contrast, the current trial employed a shortened four-cycle R-DHAOx regimen, leveraging BTK inhibitor-based induction and maintenance to reduce cumulative chemotherapy exposure and HDT/ASCT.

In this trial, the overall CR rate was 88%, as assessed based on PET scan using the 2014 Lugano criteria32. In contrast, the LyMa trial2 (R-DHA-platinum regimen) and MCL Younger trial27 (alternating R-CHOP and R-DHAP) reported a CR rate, including unconfirmed CR of 77% and 55%, respectively, assessed based on CT scan using the 1999 International Working Group criteria33. In the TRIANGLE trial using alternating R-CHOP and R-DHAP/R-DHAOx4, the CR rate was 45% with ibrutinib and 36% without ibrutinib based on CT scan using the 2007 revised criteria34. Direct cross-trial comparisons should be interpreted with caution, given differences in response criteria and imaging modalities. Additionally, according to the post-hoc subgroup analyses, patients with classic/small cell disease and wild-type TP53 may benefit more from zanubrutinib-rituximab induction and R-DHAOx chemotherapy. No significant differences were observed based on other established prognostic markers, such as Ki-67, Ann Arbor stage, and sMIPI risk. Further randomized controlled trials should be conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the proposed treatment regimen in this trial.

Compared with the WINDOW-1 trial21, patients in this trial had numerically higher percentage of Ki-67 ≥ 30%, higher MIPI risk, but lower rate of TP53 mutation. The duration of induction treatment was also shorter in this trial (median cycles: 4 vs 7). Despite these differences, the response to zanubrutinib-rituximab induction in this trial (CR, 88%; ORR, 98%) was similar to that reported for ibrutinib plus rituximab in the WINDOW-1 trial (CR, 87%; ORR, 98%). The fewer induction cycles required to achieve CR may reflect improved efficacy or, alternatively, differences in response assessment methodology (responses were assessed using PET scans routinely after cycle 4 in this trial, but only used to verify CR after CT screening in the WINDOW-1 trial). Temporal pattern of treatment failure also differed: all five PD events in this trial occurred within nine months of treatment initiation; in contrast, the PD events in the WINDOW-1 trial occurred over a much longer period, even after 24 months. This difference might be related to the maintenance therapy with zanubrutinib following chemoimmunotherapy in our trial, but an extended follow-up is warranted since the median follow-up was only 23 months.

None of the patients in this trial required a dose reduction of zanubrutinib during zanubrutinib-rituximab induction treatment. In contrast, one-third of patients in the WINDOW-1 trial required a dose reduction of ibrutinib due to AEs. Such a difference may reflect a more favorable safety profile with the zanubrutinib-rituximab regimen than ibrutinib plus rituximab. Additionally, this difference could also be attributable to the shorter induction cycles in our trial.

A recent phase II trial reported 80% CR rate when using the ibrutinib-rituximab regimen in treating untreated indolent clinical forms of MCL (non-blastoid variants, Ki-67 ≤ 30%, asymptomatic disease, ECOG 0-1, and largest lesion diameter ≤ 3 cm)16. Five out of 42 patients in the current trial had untreated indolent clinical forms of MCL using the same criteria, and all achieved CR. In addition, our trial included nine patients aged 65–75 years and achieved a CR rate of 88% in this group of patients. In previous trials for MCL patients of 65 years of age or older, the ibrutinib-rituximab regimen resulted in a CR rate of 71%17, whereas the CR rate in patients receiving the BR regimen with or without BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib or acalabrutinib) was 65.5–66.6% and 53.5–57.6%8,35. A phase II trial investigating BR plus low-dose cytarabine regimen in MCL patients aged > 65 years or 60-65 years but ineligible for HDT/ASCT reported a CR rate of 91% at the end of treatment36.

As an exploratory analysis in our study, unsupervised hierarchical clustering identified three molecular subtypes. The M1 subtype was characterized by enrichment of cell cycle pathways and MYC-targets signatures. All four patients of M1 subtype did not achieve CR in part A. This finding is consistent with a previous study showing poor clinical outcomes in patients with an MCL subtype characterized by cell cycle and MYC pathways activation37. The M2 subtype was associated with activation of T cells and accounted for the majority of the patients with early-CR. In the WINDOW-1 trial, a molecular subtype similar to M2 also had a higher rate of early-CR and exhibited significant activation of immune-related pathways, while the non-CR subgroup was characterized by the enrichment of MYC pathway and BCR signaling pathway, which is similar to the M1 subtype in this trial21. The M3 subtype exhibited features of a more complex tumor-microenvironment with upregulation of inflammatory pathways, higher infiltration of stromal cells, and immunosuppressive cells. All patients of the M3 subtype achieved CR during part A of this trial, but required more treatment cycles than the M2 subtype. It has also been reported that an immune-depleted microenvironment was associated with resistance to BTK inhibitors38. Additionally, the fact that all patients of the M2 subtype in this trial had MRD-negative CR at the completion of part A encourages future studies of chemotherapy-free therapy in this patient subpopulation. Molecular and genetic testing may play a crucial role in identifying the patient population suitable for chemotherapy-free strategies in future research.

This trial had several limitations. First, the trial did not have a control group. Interpretation of the findings in the context of standard therapies remains limited. Second, the sample size is relatively small. Accordingly, the results must be considered preliminary and verified in future studies with larger sample sizes. Third, in the molecular subtype analyses, the absence of multivariable analysis and independent validation has resulted in a reduced reliability of the findings, necessitating further verification.

In conclusion, frontline treatment with zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by a shortened R-DHAOx chemoimmunotherapy and zanubrutinib maintenance achieved a high CR rate in patients with previously untreated MCL. Although the induction and maintenance phases were generally well-tolerated, myelosuppression remained the main toxicity during the chemoimmunotherapy phase. Future randomized controlled trials are required to validate frontline strategies that minimize chemotherapy use in MCL.

sec.title: Trial design and patients
sec.p: This trial protocol was approved by the ethics committees of participating centers (the Ethics committee of Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, the Ethics Committee of Huizhou Municipal Central Hospital, and ethics committee of the Second Hospital of Dalian Medical University). The trial was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki and all relevant regulations regarding the use of human study participants. All patients provided written informed consent. The consent to publish clinical information potentially identifying individuals was obtained. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04624958 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04624958; first posted on November 12, 2020).

This investigator-initiated, single-arm, phase II trial (CHESS) was conducted in three centers in China. This was an open-label trial. Participants, investigators, attending physicians, and outcome assessors were not blinded. Previously untreated patients aged 18–75 years with histologically confirmed, Ann Arbor stage II-IV MCL, requiring immediate anti-lymphoma treatment, were eligible. Additional inclusion criteria included: ECOG performance status score of 0 to 2, at least one measurable lesion, and adequate organ and bone marrow function. Patients were excluded if they had central nervous system involvement, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, a history of active bleeding or hemorrhagic diathesis, or required treatment with anticoagulants or strong CYP3A inhibitors. The full list of inclusion and exclusion criteria is presented in the trial protocol in the supplementary notes.

sec.title: Study treatment
sec.p: The treatment consisted of three phases. A treatment schema describing the study treatment process is presented in Supplementary Fig. 7. In part A (induction phase), zanubrutinib (160 mg, twice a day, orally) and rituximab (375 mg/m2, intravenously on day 1) were administered in 28-day cycles until CR, disease progression, or unacceptable toxicity, with a maximum of 12 cycles. In part B (chemoimmunotherapy phase), R-DHAOx (rituximab 375 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1; dexamethasone 20 mg intravenously on days 1–4; cytarabine 2 g/m2 intravenously on days 2–3 [1 g/m2 for patients > 65 years of age]; and oxaliplatin 130 mg/m2 intravenously on day (1) was administered in 21-day cycles until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity, with a maximum of four cycles. In the maintenance phase, zanubrutinib (160 mg orally, twice a day) was given until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity for up to one year. Unacceptable toxicity was defined as meeting any of the criteria for dose discontinuation of zanubrutinib or chemotherapeutic drugs as described in the protocol during treatment, or if continued treatment is deemed inappropriate by the investigators.

Patients achieving CR or PD in part A proceeded to part B; patients with PR or stable disease (SD) in part A received 12 cycles of zanubrutinib-rituximab treatment prior to proceeding to part B. Patients with CR at part B completion proceeded to the maintenance phase; young patients (≤65 years) with detectable MRD were eligible for ASCT before maintenance. Patients with PR, SD, or PD at part B completion were taken off the trial.

sec.title: Assessments and endpoints
sec.p: Responses were evaluated by the investigators every two cycles in part A and part B, and every three cycles during maintenance therapy using PET or computerized tomography (CT) according to the Lugano 2014 criteria32. A bone marrow biopsy is required to confirm CR in patients with bone marrow involvement at baseline. Safety assessment was performed on all patient visits. Adverse events (AEs) were graded according to the National Cancer Institute’s Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (version 5.0).

MRD in bone marrow and/or peripheral blood was measured using flow cytometry with a sensitivity of 10−4 at baseline and upon the completion of part A and part B. Bone marrow aspiration was performed at completion of part A and part B in patients with bone marrow involvement at baseline, but not routinely in patients without bone marrow involvement at baseline. The collection of peripheral blood for MRD evaluation was performed at baseline and upon the completion of part A and part B. Detectable MRD in either bone marrow or peripheral blood was considered MRD-positive.

The primary endpoint was the CR rate at the completion of part A in the intention-to-treat population, defined as the proportion of patients with CR. Secondary endpoints included overall response (proportion of patients with CR plus PR), MRD, PFS, OS, DoR, time to CR, and adverse events for part A, part B, and maintenance phase. PFS was defined as the time from treatment initiation to disease progression or death, whichever occurs earlier, and was censored at the last follow-up date in alive patients without disease progression. OS was defined as the time from treatment initiation to patient death or the last follow-up. DoR was defined as the time from first response to disease progression or death, whichever occurs earlier. Time to CR was defined as the time from treatment initiation to the first documentation of CR.

sec.title: RNA-seq and transcriptomic analyses
sec.p: Total RNA from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor samples obtained at baseline was extracted using the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen). RNA purity was assessed using Nanodrop 2000 for A260/280 and A260/A230 ratios (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All RNA samples were quantified by Qubit 3.0 using the RNA BR Assay Kit (Life Technologies). RNA integrity was assessed using Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent). A RIN value (RNA integrity number) higher than 6.5 was required. RNA sequencing libraries were prepared using the KAPA Stranded RNA-Seq Kit with RiboErase (KAPA Biosystems). Final library was quantified using KAPA Library Quantification Kit (KAPA Biosystems), and sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq4000 platform using PE150 sequencing chemistry (Illumina, USA) to an average of 50 M reads per sample.

FASTQ file quality control was performed using Trimmomatic39, where N bases and low-quality (score <15) bases were removed. Reads aligning to rRNA and tRNA sequences were removed. Cleaned reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg19) using STAR v 2.5.2b40. Transcripts were quantified using RSEM41, which uses an expectation maximization algorithm to optimally assign reads that map to multiple transcripts.

Based on treatment response at the completion of part A, we categorized the patients into three groups: early-CR (achieving CR within four cycles of the zanubrutinib-rituximab regimen), late-CR (achieving CR after more than four cycles of the zanubrutinib-rituximab regimen), and non-CR. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between non-CR, late-CR, and early-CR tumors were identified using the edgeR package (v4.3.16) with its default parameters. DEGs were defined as genes with |log2(fold change)| > 0.5 and P-value < 0.01. RNA-seq data were deconvolved with the ESTIMATE algorithm (v1.0.13) in R software and the TIDE algorithm (v1.3) in Python 3.12.7 software for immune infiltration analyses.

Samples were classified into three subtypes based on the normalized FPKM values of DEGs by applying an unsupervised hierarchical clustering method. When performing unsupervised hierarchical clustering, we calculated the distance matrix using the Euclidean distance metric (dist function with method = “euclidean”) and applied the hclust function with the Ward’s minimum variance method (method = “ward.D”), which minimizes the total within-cluster variance. The results were visualized using a dendrogram to represent the hierarchical structure of the clusters. To specify a desired number of clusters, we used the cutree function to cut the dendrogram. To visualize subtype characteristics, a heat map was generated using the ComplexHeatmap R package (v2.21.1) based on normalized FPKM values of DEGs. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of Hallmark and Reactome pathways, and Gene Ontology terms were performed using the clusterProfiler R package (v4.13.3) based on pre-ranked differentially expressed gene panels of each subtype. Single-sample GSVA scores of GOBP, Hallmark, and Reactome gene sets in the MSigDB database (v2024.1.Hs) were calculated using the GSVA R package (v1.53.23), and the representative significantly enriched pathways in the three subtypes were plotted using the pheatmap R package (v1.0.12).

sec.title: DNA sequencing and genomic analyses
sec.p: DNA from FFPE tissue and matched germline samples were extracted using a DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen). Purified DNAs were quality checked using Nanodrop 2000 for A260/280 and A260/A230 ratios (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All DNA samples were quantified by Qubit 3.0 using the dsDNA HS Assay Kit (Life Technologies). Sequencing libraries were prepared using the KAPA Hyper Prep Kit (KAPA Biosystems). Target enrichment was performed using the xGen Exome Research Panel and Hybridization and Wash Reagents Kit (Integrated DNA Technology, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Libraries were subjected to PCR amplification with KAPA HiFi Hot-Start ReadyMix (KAPA Biosystems). The purified library was quantified using the KAPA Library Quantification Kit (KAPA Biosystems), and its fragment size distribution was analyzed using a Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent). Sequencing was performed on the Illumina HiSeq4000 platform using PE150 sequencing chemistry (Illumina, USA).

FASTQ file quality control was performed using Trimmomatic39, where N bases and low-quality (score <20) bases were removed. Pair-end reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg37) using Burrows-Wheeler Aligner (BWA) with default parameters, followed by PCR deduplication with Picard V2.9.4 (Broad Institute, MA, USA). Local realignment around indels and base quality score recalibration were performed with the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK 3.4.0). Somatic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) were identified using VarDict and MuTect2 for matched tumor-normal samples, and TNhaplotyper2 for tumor-only samples. To eliminate sequencing artifacts and common germline events in tumor-only samples, both SNVs and small insertions/deletions (indels) were filtered using an in-house common variant database that includes 2000 whole-exome sequencing (WES) normal samples. The final list of mutations was annotated using vcf2maf (available on GitHub). The resulting mutation list was filtered through an internal list. Somatic mutation calls were further filtered using the following criteria: (i) minimum 4 reads supporting the variant; (ii) ≥ 2% variant allele frequency (VAF); (iii) not present in public databases (Exome Variant Server, 1,000 genomes project, and Exome Aggregation Consortium) at population frequency > 1%; (iv) in protein-coding regions. Oncoprint, constructed by R (3.5.3), was used to view the overall mutation landscape of patients. Tumor mutation burden (TMB) was counted by summing all base substitutions and indels in the coding region of targeted genes, including synonymous alterations to reduce sampling noise and excluding known driver mutations as they are over-represented in the panel42.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Sample size was estimated according to a single-stage phase 2 design based on the following assumptions: (1) CR rate of 70% for historical control2 and 90% with the regimen in this trial; (2) 90% power and two-sided 5% type I error; (3) a dropout rate of 10%. The calculation yielded 42 patients.

Response assessment was performed in the full analysis set (ITT population) and per protocol set. Safety assessment was performed in the safety analysis sets, which were divided into three datasets and each contained patients who received the study treatment at least once in part A, part B, or the maintenance phase.

Descriptive statistics were used to present baseline characteristics, response rates, and the rate of AEs. The 95% confidence interval (CI) of rates was calculated using the Clopper-Pearson method. Survival outcomes and 95% CIs were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. The 2-year PFS and OS were calculated. The log-rank test was used to evaluate the difference in PFS and OS between subgroups. Post-hoc analyses included the subgroup analyses of CR rate at part A completion, CR rate at part B completion, PFS, and OS. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 25.0), R software (version 3.6.1), and Python (version 3.12.7). Two-sided P of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
